overview: This atlas label groups Central Asian khanates across 1530 to 1914, but its polygons are misplaced or conflated: the earliest lies in the Arctic, and later outlines combine widely separated regions. They cannot show reliable state boundaries. This regional account focuses on the separate states of Bukhara, Khiva and, from the eighteenth century, Kokand. Their rulers governed oasis cities, farms and pastoral communities through changing dynasties and alliances. They never formed one khanate lasting throughout the map interval.

periods.title: Earlier khanates and divided authority
periods.summary: Shibanid and successor rulers governed territories through royal relatives, military leaders and religious institutions.

periods.title: Kokand and regional rivalry
periods.summary: Kokand emerged in Ferghana beside older Bukhara and Khiva, expanding irrigation, trade and political power.

periods.title: Russian domination and unequal survival
periods.summary: Conquest brought different outcomes: annexation in Kokand, subordinate monarchies in Bukhara and Khiva.

items.text: Sixteenth-century government often rested on a ruling family sharing authority. Princes controlled territories called appanages, including Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent and Balkh. A khan had to manage powerful relatives and military supporters. An impressive title did not automatically make every cousin obey.

Bukhara’s rulers also invested in city life. In the 1530s and 1540s, Abd al-Aziz rebuilt walls and supported religious buildings; the Mir Arab madrasa was completed in 1535. A school, a shrine and a defensive wall served different needs within the same urban landscape.

The khanates did not collect taxes in identical ways. In nineteenth-century Bukhara, provincial governors handled collection. In Khiva’s more centralized system, officials sent by the central government collected taxes once or twice a year. Irrigation, local authority and royal revenue were closely connected.

Kokand grew partly through migration. During the eighteenth century, people arriving from Samarkand, Kashgar, nearby mountains and the steppe brought labor and skills into Ferghana. Some fled violence elsewhere. The expanding state depended on a mixture of settled farmers and townspeople, pastoral groups and merchants.

Kokand’s dealings with Qing China combined diplomacy, military pressure and trade. Rulers sought economic advantages for merchants in Xinjiang. Officials on each side could interpret their relationship differently, so diplomatic language sometimes left room for negotiation rather than settling exactly who answered to whom.

In the 1810s, Omar Khan ordered canals near Namangan and in southeastern Ferghana. A new town, Shahrikhan, followed in 1815 to 1816. Irrigation helped create farmland for a growing population, while rulers hoped that migrants and refugees would become tax-paying subjects.

Khiva’s surviving domestic architecture includes enclosed courtyards, private rooms and reception areas with carved wooden posts. UNESCO describes versions spanning the eighteenth to twentieth centuries. These houses preserve places for family life and receiving visitors alongside the city’s much more conspicuous palaces.

Bukhara had sixteen public baths in 1848, according to its heritage evaluation. Washing therefore had a place in the city’s shared institutions. The number belongs to this particular nineteenth-century city, not every oasis settlement.

An early nineteenth-century Bukhara embroidered cover introduces a family project. Relatives could embroider separate strips of a bride’s suzani, then sew them together. Slightly mismatched joins preserved the teamwork: beautiful decoration did not require every flower to line up perfectly.

A photograph catalogued by the Library of Congress shows tea stalls along a Samarkand street, with a ruined mosque behind them. Dated between 1865 and 1872, it records everyday commerce around the transition to Russian rule. The city’s history included places to buy a drink as well as royal monuments.

sections.title: Learning within families and beyond them

items.text: Delshad Barna’s life makes the costs of expansion personal. In her own account, she lost her parents as a child and was taken from Ura Tepe to Kokand during a military assault in 1816. Her later writing combined memories of displacement with the history of the khanate.

After marrying in 1820, Delshad taught at her mother-in-law’s girls’ school in Kokand. Her mother-in-law also introduced her to Chaghatay language and literature; Delshad said she had previously spoken only Persian. Education could pass between adult family members as well as from teachers to children.

In 1830, Delshad opened her own girls’ school, teaching reading and writing over a long career. Her surviving works include poetry in Persian and Chaghatay and a historical memoir. These records preserve a woman’s contribution to education beyond the better-known literary circles at court.

sections.title: Objects, skilled hands and written words

items.text: A nineteenth-century Kokand horse outfit in the Metropolitan Museum combines leather, silver, turquoise, carnelian, enamel and textile. Its bridle and other fittings brought several crafts together. This was elaborate equipment: the horse could arrive wearing rather more jewelry than its rider’s spectators.

Visiting Kokand in 1873, Eugene Schuyler found mint workers making silver ornaments for bridles and harnesses. He was told that the mint master also served as court jeweller. The same workshop skills could turn precious metal into money or an impressive horse accessory.

Schuyler also described Khudayar Khan’s palace front covered in white, blue and green glazed tiles. He saw only the facade briefly and was not admitted inside. His account preserves a contemporary impression of architectural display while making the limits of his visit unusually clear.

“ضرب بخارا”, transliterated zarb Bukhara, means “struck at Bukhara”. Torrey prints this mint phrase on Nasr Allah’s gold coin dated AH 1257. It uses Arabic script in the Persian coinage tradition. The lettering here follows a modern transcription of the nineteenth-century object.

ending.text: Russian conquest eliminated Kokand’s khanate in 1876. Bukhara and Khiva survived as subordinate monarchies beyond the map’s 1914 endpoint, until 1920. Their cities, families, languages and crafts continued under profoundly changed governments.
